reason: Linear capsules are normal (Brassicaceae siliques, Onagraceae and others).
A gland or secretory area can be broad. The examples are about glands, so the part mapping is a little loose.
The examples describe hyalocysts and a hyaline hairpoint, not the costa. This is a wrong part reading. A hyaline costa itself is rare.
The examples are about the sheath summit or apex, not the whole leaf. A rule would need to assign the shape to the apex or summit instead of the leaf.
Spikes can droop or nod.
Perigynium beaks are toothed (bidentulate), so this is correct for sedges.
Perigynium wall thickness (thin) is a real character in Carex.
PATO 'characteristic' is the root term and too generic. The examples are 'or' alternatives (stout or slender, erect or reflexed) that need specific terms.
Spikelets can be ellipsoid. Ellipsoid reads as prolate here.
'Spatial pattern' is a generic parent. The examples mix imbricate (arrangement) and reticulate (surface pattern), so each needs its own specific term.
Mealy or farinose bark or surface is a real descriptor.
Lobes and blades can be elliptic.
Leaf sheaths can be dilated.
Hemispheric stigmas are common.
A persistent receptacle is a normal fruit character.
Discs and similar surfaces can have ridges.
Fimbriate margins on bracteoles are normal.
The bract surface can have a colour.
Ray flowers (corolla tubes) can be hairy.
A narrow stem is fine, but the examples describe sheath scars, cavities and branches. A rule would need to check that 'narrow' applies to the stem itself.
Filaments can be terete.
Leaf margins can be setose.
Rostellum lobes can be curved.
The viscidium has a shape. Shape is the attribute for the specific shape values.
A surface can have a hair covering (pilosity) such as puberulent or glabrous.
A surface can have a colour.
Hemispheric receptacles occur (for example in Asteraceae).
Sporophylls can be glabrous.
Lobes, margins and bases can be narrow.
Papillose is a surface texture.
'Characteristic' is the generic root term. The examples are 'or' alternatives (caudate or acuminate) that need specific shape terms.
Samaras have colours.
The abaxial epidermis can be hispidulous.

The examples include comparatives ('longer than upper ones') and measurements ('up to 2 cm long'), not only the quality 'long'. A rule would need to split measurements and comparisons from the qualitative term.
Pubescent hair cover is normal for plant surfaces.
Fruits (achenes) can be variegated or multi-coloured.
Semiorbicular leaf shape is a normal term, though some examples refer to the base or leaf scars.
Anthers can be square in outline.
Branches can be herbaceous.
Leaf margins and apices can be fimbriate.
A midvein can be broad.
Parallelodromous is a venation pattern of the whole leaf. The examples say the tertiary veins run parallel to each other, which is a different meaning.
Awns can be reflexed.
Pseudobulbs can be fusiform.
'1-3 cm apart' is the spacing between pseudobulbs, not an amount. This is a wrong reading, and a spacing rule is needed.
Lobes can be elliptic.
The examples describe a spur (an orchid or flower spur) that was mapped to short shoot. This is a wrong part reading.
Lobes can be pointed.
Plicae have a shape.
A persistent stylopodium is normal in Apiaceae. There is only one flora, so it is less certain.
Staminodes can be papillate.
Glumes can be small.
Leaf sheaths can be flattened.
Sinuses have a width.
Pubescent hair cover is normal for tubes and surfaces.
Nectar scales can be linear.
Cataphylls have a position (basal, remote).
Traps (bladders) can be ovoid, and ovate is the closest PATO term.
A receptacle can have a depth (a concave receptacle).
An endostome has a colour.
